newsitem.title: USA: Bush Jr. says too early to think about presidency.
newsitem.headline: Bush Jr. says too early to think about presidency.

text.p: Texas Gov. George Bush, son of the former president, says he is flattered many Republicans see him as presidential material but insists it is too early to think about the White House.
In an interview with Reuters on Monday, Bush said he was totally focused on Texas and particularly on a plan he presented last week to cut property taxes in the state.
"Of course, when people ask you (about running for president) and there's speculation, I'm aware of it. You can't help but be flattered," Bush said.

"But it's important to distinguish beween flattery and reality. It's wonderful when people say nice things about you. But understand, that doesn't exist forever. This is a tough business we're in," he said.

"The other thing flattery can do is take you off mission. My mission is Texas," he added. "So I don't allow the speculation to lure me off the job in hand, which in this case is cutting the property taxes of Texas."
Bush, 50, is seen by many Republicans as one of their brightest presidential prospects for 2000. This week, the conservative magazine, The Standard, put him on the cover.

In a Reuters poll last week, Bush was second among Republican voters as their choice for presidential nominee, behind retired Gen. Colin Powell and ahead of figures like 1996 vice presidential candidate Jack Kemp and former Vice President Dan Quayle.

First, however, Bush must decide whether to run for re-election as governor of Texas in 1998. He said he would announce his decision in July, when he would also answer questions about his presidential ambitions.

"I'm obviously going to have to answer that question. At the press conference after I announce my intentions that will probably be the second question. I will answer that question then because I need to make up my mind first if I'm going to run for governor," Bush said.

Crucial to his future is the tax plan he announced last week, which would cut property taxes by around 40 percent but would increase the state sales tax by half a cent and also introduce a new tax on lawyers, accountants, doctors and others who belong to professional partnerships.
The plan has already attracted opposition from some conservatives, who oppose any tax increases, and political analysts say Bush is taking a considerable political risk.
"If there are any risks, I don't care. I have a wonderful sense of freedom knowing this is right for my state. It has to happen and this is the right time for it to happen," he said.

Bush said he had no illusions about the demands of the presidency and did not dream of having the job. "I've seen the good side and I've seen the bad side. I come with a very realistic view of the presidency," he said.

"I was eldest son to a great man who was president of the United States. I was close during some monumental historic achievements. I was in the room the day he was defeated. To me, it's not a fantasy, it was reality."

While some Republicans are already beginning to organise themselves for a presidential run, Bush said he had taken no steps to position himself. "I'm not trying to do that. I stay at home, I'm doing my business. I've never been yelling on one of these TV shows, saying, 'look how important I am.'"
